transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-05 16:30 UTC | Duration: 52m
Attendees: Sam Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Acme Lead Eng), Priya Malhotra (Acme Platform), Jordan Lee (Acme CTO)

-- Auto-summary (auto-generated): Walkthrough of SDK quickstarts. Customer wants concrete steps to wire up API keys from Vault, run a local quickstart with Python and Node, and see basic console observability.

[00:00:00] Sam (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, and then we'll jump into a live walkthrough of the SDKs — Python and TypeScript. Maya will lead the code bits. Alex, Priya, Jordan — anything to flag up front?
[00:00:12] Alex (Acme): No, thanks Sam. We're mainly here to see a developer quick path: how to authenticate securely, run a sample request, and what the console looks like. Also curious about Dedicated for PHI workloads later.
[00:00:25] Jordan (Acme CTO): Yep, and timeline — if we like it, we want a pilot within the next 3–4 weeks.
[00:00:30] Maya (Redwood SE): Great. Today's plan: 1) quick env setup for Python and Node; 2) run a simple generation and streaming example; 3) cover auth best practices (api key vs service token + using Vault/KMS); 4) show Console traces and Optimize suggestions; 5) Q&A + next steps.

[00:01:05] Sam: Also we'll drop links in chat: quickstart repo, security whitepaper, and an example env file.
[00:01:10] Priya (Acme): Perfect. How long is the quickstart repo? We have strict change windows and would prefer tiny footprint to demo first.
[00:01:18] Maya: The repo has two folders — python/ and ts/ — each with a one-file quickstart and a README. The python quickstart is ~25 lines; Node is similar. We'll share a script that uses env vars so you can plug in secrets from Vault.

[00:02:05] Maya: Alright I'm going to share my screen — starting with the README. Step one: pip install redwood-inference (note: package name in repo). Then set REDWOOD_API_KEY or use a service token injected at runtime.
[00:02:28] Alex: Is the SDK published to PyPI and npm?
[00:02:31] Maya: Yes, PyPI and npm. We'll include exact versions in the repo. For teams that prefer not to store a long-lived API key on disk, we recommend short-lived service tokens and a secrets manager — e.g., HashiCorp Vault or cloud KMS.
[00:02:45] Jordan: Quick question on scopes — can we restrict service tokens to only generation endpoints or embeddings?
[00:02:51] Maya: Yes, tokens can be scoped by route and model. We also support role-based access controls via the Console for team members.

[00:03:20] Maya: Running the python example now. Code: import redwood; client = redwood.Client(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — then client.generate .... (note: transcript has small errors here).
[00:03:45] Alex: That looks straightforward. What about streaming? We need to do partial output to our web socket stream.
[00:03:52] Maya: For streaming in Python we expose a .stream() method that yields chunks. In Node the SDK emits 'data' events. I'll run the stream example — you'll see the UI update as tokens arrive.
[00:04:20] [screen noise, brief pause]
[00:04:40] Maya: One caveat — long polling is handled by the runtime, and for ultra-low latency you can use the 'realtime' path in dedicated deployments. Hosted streaming is good up to ~200ms token latency depending on model.
[00:04:58] Priya: Is there an example using websockets from the client?
[00:05:05] Maya: Yes, in ts/examples/realtime-ws.ts — uses the same auth header pattern. We'll add a snippet to the README for your infra team.

[00:05:40] Sam: Let's cover environment setup for CI/CD. Acme, do you provision secrets using Vault today?
[00:05:48] Priya: Yes, HashiCorp Vault with dynamic secrets for DBs, but for third party APIs we usually pull a short-lived token via a ci-runner role.
[00:05:57] Sam: Perfect match. Our recommended pattern: short-lived service tokens created by the Console or the Private control plane and rotated via Vault. We have example terraform modules and a small action in the repo for retrieving and injecting the token.
[00:06:15] Alex: Any gotchas on TLS or cert pinning for private deployments?
[00:06:20] Maya: For Private (VPC/on-prem) we offer mTLS options and you can use your own certs; for Hosted we support TLS with public certs. There's also a network whitelist option for Dedicated. We'll send the architecture doc.

[00:07:00] Maya: Now switching to the Console — here's the per-route dashboard. You can see request latencies, per-token cost breakout, and an example trace that shows batching and cache hits.
[00:07:18] Alex: That cost breakdown looks useful. Where does the per-token charge show — do you break out embedding vs generation?
[00:07:25] Maya: Yes, the Console separates token generation cost, embedding units, and compute. The Optimize tab will recommend batching and quantization profiles based on your request shape.

[00:08:05] Jordan: On Optimize — can it recommend model variants automatically for throughput vs quality?
[00:08:12] Maya: It suggests compatible quantized builds or smaller model variants for a given prompt set and latency target. It's a guidance engine — you still review before applying.

[00:09:00] Alex: Back to SDK specifics: error handling. If we hit rate limits or transient GPU OOMs, what's the recommended retry pattern?
[00:09:08] Maya: We expose standardized error classes. For 429 — exponential backoff with jitter. For 503/5xx — retry with capped backoff and fallback to smaller model variant if available. We also support automatic fallback policies in the routing layer.

[00:09:45] Priya: Can we capture trace IDs in our logs to correlate with Redwood traces?
[00:09:51] Maya: Yes, every request returns a request_id and trace_id in headers — pass it into your logs. The Console links traces to the request_id so you can pivot from application logs.

[00:10:20] Sam: Quick note on compliance: we have SOC2 details in the security whitepaper; for encrypted-at-rest keys we integrate with KMS/HSM, though sometimes the transcript has Kay-mess miswritten.
[00:10:33] Priya: Good. For PHI, we'll likely need Private on-prem or a Dedicated VPC with a BAA. Is that doable?
[00:10:40] Maya: Yes, we offer Private and Dedicated; brings extra isolation and optionally an on-prem package for air-gapped setups. We'll include the BAA process in the security packet.

[00:11:10] Alex: Let's try a code change: modify prompt templates and re-run local tests. How does caching affect dev iteration?
[00:11:18] Maya: We have prefix/KV caching at the runtime. In dev you can disable caching via a per-request header or set debug=true in the SDK to bypass cache. For CI you might want deterministic outputs — we recommend a consistent seed option in the SDK.

[00:12:05] Maya: I'm now opening the node quickstart. npm install @redwood/inference (note: package name). Example usage: const client = new Redwood.Client({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); client.chat.create({ model: 'rw-medium-1', messages: [...] }) — streaming via client.chat.stream() with event emitter.
[00:12:34] Alex: If we migrate later to Dedicated, do we need to change code or just swap endpoint and API key?
[00:12:40] Maya: It's a smooth swap — same SDK, you just point to a different base_url and use the Dedicated credential. Rollouts and pinning happen at the control plane so clients can remain unchanged.

[00:13:10] Priya: Any CLI tooling for quick environment checks?
[00:13:14] Sam: We have a small 'rwctl' CLI in the repo that can validate env, check auth, and run a sample request.

[00:13:40] Jordan: Let's talk quotas and rate limiting for the pilot — for example 20 concurrent streams and baseline throughput.
[00:13:48] Sam: For hosted we can request soft quota increases for trial, and for Dedicated you reserve GPU capacity. We'll propose a pilot package in the follow-up pricing note.

[00:14:20] Maya: Heading into a short demo of the Console trace: here's a sample latency waterfall that highlights batching at the runtime. You can toggle cache visualization to see KV hits. Note, sometimes the auto-transcript has K-V cash which is mis-typed.
[00:14:45] Alex: Nice. Do you expose the batching window config via API?
[00:14:52] Maya: Yes, batching and autoscale policies are configurable per deployment in Dedicated, and in Hosted we expose a suggested profile and Optimize will push recommendations.

[00:15:20] Sam: Quick pause for questions.
[00:15:28] Alex: On auth rotation: can the service token be minted via an internal service account with a short TTL?
[00:15:34] Maya: Exactly. We support token minting endpoints; you can call them from a trusted server which gets identity from your KMS or OIDC provider. Tokens can be 5–30 min TTL.

[00:16:00] Priya: Regarding logs retention — how long are request bodies retained? We need to meet data residency rules and retention windows.
[00:16:07] Sam: By default hosted retains logs for 30 days, but enterprise plans can configure retention and retention rules. Private deployments can be configured to retain logs per your policy or forward logs to your SIEM.

[00:16:40] Maya: Code snippet for retry middleware in node — simple example uses axios-retry style logic. Also we emit structured errors with code fields so you can automate fallback to cached responses or a simpler LLM.

[00:17:20] Jordan: On monitoring, can we get per-tenant cost export to our billing system?
[00:17:27] Maya: Yes, billing exports and per-token cost reports are available via API and CSV. You can pipe those into your cost system.

[00:18:00] Alex: One more on streaming: do you support delta updates for embeddings or partial rerank signals?
[00:18:08] Maya: For embeddings we don't stream partial embeddings — they are computed as a single unit. For reranking you can stream candidate scores when using the rerank API.

[00:18:40] Sam: Ok, we're at about 18 minutes into the call; going to speed run the quickstart test from local — Maya will run python then node and show the Console updating.
[00:18:56] [keyboard clicks; short silence]
[00:19:20] Maya: Python quickstart ran — here's the response (shows token stream). Console shows request_id rwd_1234 and a latency 142ms for this sample.
[00:19:32] Alex: 142ms is good. What model was that?
[00:19:35] Maya: That was a small 'rw-small-1' quantized build — lower cost, lower quality than our flagship. Optimize suggested it based on prompt length.

[00:20:05] Priya: If we do a canary rollout of a new prompt template, can Console automatically compare quality metrics?
[00:20:12] Maya: Yes — you can attach an eval set and Console will compute regression alerts if quality drops. We support promptsets and eval harnesses.

[00:20:45] Jordan: Security question: SSO and RBAC — can we map groups from our IdP to Console roles?
[00:20:51] Sam: Yes, SAML/SSO is supported; you can sync groups and map to RBAC roles. We'll include a sample SAML config in the security packet.

[00:21:20] Alex: Any rate-limiting on embeddings that we should watch?
[00:21:26] Maya: Embeddings are metered separately and we can set per-route quotas. For high throughput embedding pipelines we recommend batching on your side and using our batch embeddings endpoint to reduce overhead.

[00:22:00] Priya: For the pilot, we'd like a sandbox account with restricted scopes and a small Dedicated quota to validate network setup. How long does provisioning take?
[00:22:08] Sam: Hosted sandbox can be provisioned within a day. Dedicated trial needs a bit more time — typically 3–7 business days for capacity and network setup, depending on region. We'll prioritize the network deep-dive to scope exact time.

[00:23:10] Maya: One small demo of the Optimize tab — it surfaced batching suggestions and a quantization flag. We can show sample perf delta in a spreadsheet (linked in chat).
[00:23:28] Alex: Please share that spreadsheet. We want to understand unit economics.

[00:23:40] Sam: We'll share runbooks and the benchmark spreadsheet after the call.

[00:24:05] Maya: Any final technical questions?
[00:24:12] Alex: What about SDK language parity — do Python and TS cover all new feature flags?
[00:24:18] Maya: Feature parity is close but occasionally TS gets real-time features slightly earlier. We keep a changelog in the repo. If you need parity for a pilot we'll prioritize backporting.

[00:24:40] Priya: Can we run the SDK behind our API gateway and terminate TLS at the gateway?
[00:24:46] Maya: Yes, that pattern is common. Just ensure that request headers with auth are forwarded. For some Dedicated topologies you might place a NAT gateway in front.

[00:25:10] Sam: Quick recap and next steps: Sam will share repo and pricing note; Maya will schedule deep dive; Acme to send prompt set and SLAs. Anything to add?
[00:25:25] Alex: No, that's it. Thanks.
[00:25:28] Jordan: Thanks all.
